body: Campbell, Ramadorai and Ranish, 'Getting Better or Feeling Better? How Equity Investors Respond to Investment Experience' (NBER w20000, 2014; ~55 citations), a large representative sample of Indian retail equity accounts from depository (NSDL) data, many of them new investors. Years of experience and the investor's own returns both change behaviour. Experienced investors diversify more, turn over less and behave more as theory recommends, but strong recent returns weaken this: high trading profits raise turnover. There are style-chasing and disposition effects. Portfolios of stocks held by experienced, low-turnover investors earned high returns. Anagol, Balasubramaniam and Ramadorai, 'Endowment Effects in the Field: Evidence from India's IPO Lotteries' (Review of Economic Studies 85(4), 2018; ~60 citations): oversubscribed Indian IPOs allocate shares to retail applicants by lottery, a natural experiment. Randomly chosen winners were much more likely to still hold the stock long after, compared with losers who could have bought it on the market. This is the endowment effect and inertia, at real stakes. Their 'Learning from Noise' (Journal of Financial Economics 2021) shows that randomly higher IPO gains made investors apply for more IPOs and trade more afterwards, so people learn from luck. SEBI's F&O studies (insight:sebi-fo-losses: 87-93% of individuals lose) are the extreme form of the overconfidence and turnover penalty seen in Barber-Odean. Replicated: the experience-learning and endowment results match US and Finnish evidence. Use for us: (1) we are vulnerable to 'feeling better' after a hot streak, so lock trading frequency rules in advance; (2) holdings we received rather than chose (IPO allotments, inherited, bonus or demerger shares) must be re-underwritten as if buying fresh; (3) a stock held mostly by experienced, low-turnover owners (long-only funds, families) is a mild positive.

data.crr_finding: experience -> better behaviour; high profits -> more turnover

title: Indian retail investors: experience improves behaviour (Campbell-Ramadorai-Ranish 2014), IPO-lottery winners hold what they're given (Anagol et al.), F&O losses are the extreme case
